## Heterogeneity, model effects, and predictive performance


### Question

How much overall, warming, context, and total response-scale species heterogeneity is reduced by each information source? How well do the climate-only and six predictor models generalize to held-out transplant gradients?

### Dataset and sample size

Each information source uses the matched data and covariance from its own validated predictor sequence.

Predictive performance uses 20-fold leave-one-gradient-out validation. Trait models are evaluated on their own complete-case effects and must therefore be compared with their matched climate-only baselines rather than ranked by raw scores across traits.

### Exact model specification

Response-scale components are calculated from each full REML random covariance and compared with its matched climate-only baseline.

### Assumptions

Overall, warming, context, and total components use the registered analysis definitions; negative reductions are not truncated.

The primary performance summaries give every gradient equal influence. Effect-pooled summaries are retained as a sensitivity analysis. General-model predictions use fixed effects; repeat-species predictions additionally condition on species information learned in the training gradients. Predictive covariance includes sampling covariance, fitted species heterogeneity, and fixed-coefficient uncertainty, but treats variance-component estimates as fixed.

### Convergence and covariance diagnostics

This synthesis inherits each predictor branch's fit diagnostics and additionally requires exact component/reduction regression.

### Main numerical results

```{r}
components <- targets::tar_read(heterogeneity_components)
synthesis <- targets::tar_read(heterogeneity_synthesis)
knitr::kable(components)
knitr::kable(synthesis)
```

### Interpretation boundary

Model support and heterogeneity resolution are distinct; negative reductions are retained.

### Principal objects

`heterogeneity_components` and `heterogeneity_synthesis`.

### PASS/FAIL

Every component and reduction must be finite and pass the current release gate.

### Hierarchical model-fit R²

Marginal and conditional R² are response-scale variance partitions rather than ordinary least-squares R². Marginal R² attributes variance to fixed effects; conditional R² includes the fitted species random effects. Both denominators also include the known sampling variance.

```{r}
fit_r2 <- targets::tar_read(model_fit_r2)
knitr::kable(
  fit_r2 |>
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$aggregation == "equal_gradient",
      .data$candidate_role %in% c("standalone", "full")
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(
      "model", "n_effects", "n_species", "n_gradients",
      "marginal_R2", "conditional_R2"
    )
)
```

### Leave-gradient-out predictive performance

RMSE, MAE, bias, predictive R², Gaussian negative log predictive density, 95% prediction-interval coverage, and mean interval width are calculated from observations that were not used for their fold fit. Lower RMSE, MAE, and log score are better; bias is ideally zero; predictive R² can be negative.

```{r}
performance_metrics <- targets::tar_read(model_cross_validation_metrics)
performance_skill <- targets::tar_read(model_predictive_skill)
performance_validation <- targets::tar_read(model_performance_validation)

primary_metrics <- performance_metrics |>
  dplyr::filter(
    .data$aggregation == "equal_gradient",
    .data$support_stratum == "all",
    .data$prediction_scope == "general",
    .data$evaluation_subset == "all_eligible",
    .data$candidate_role %in% c("standalone", "full")
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    "model", "prediction_scope", "metric", "estimate", "CI_low", "CI_high",
    "n_effects", "n_species", "n_gradients"
  )
repeat_metrics <- performance_metrics |>
  dplyr::filter(
    .data$aggregation == "equal_gradient",
    .data$support_stratum == "all",
    (.data$prediction_scope == "general" &
       .data$evaluation_subset == "repeat_species") |
      (.data$prediction_scope == "repeat_species_conditional" &
         .data$evaluation_subset == "repeat_species"),
    .data$candidate_role %in% c("standalone", "full")
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    "model", "prediction_scope", "metric", "estimate", "CI_low", "CI_high",
    "n_effects", "n_species", "n_gradients"
  )
primary_skill <- performance_skill |>
  dplyr::filter(
    .data$aggregation == "equal_gradient",
    .data$support_stratum == "all",
    .data$prediction_scope == "general",
    .data$evaluation_subset == "all_eligible"
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    "model", "prediction_scope", "metric", "estimate", "CI_low", "CI_high"
  )
repeat_skill <- performance_skill |>
  dplyr::filter(
    .data$aggregation == "equal_gradient",
    .data$support_stratum == "all",
    .data$evaluation_subset == "repeat_species",
    .data$prediction_scope %in% c(
      "general", "repeat_species_conditional"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    "model", "prediction_scope", "metric", "estimate", "CI_low", "CI_high"
  )

knitr::kable(primary_metrics)
knitr::kable(primary_skill)
```

The following secondary tables compare general and conditional predictions on the identical repeat-species effects.

```{r}
knitr::kable(repeat_metrics)
knitr::kable(repeat_skill)
knitr::kable(
  performance_validation |>
    dplyr::filter(is.na(.data$heldout_gradient)) |>
    dplyr::select("check", "pass", "detail")
)
```

### Appendix figure — model fit and predictive performance

```{r, fig.width=18, fig.height=12}
targets::tar_read(appendix_model_predictive_performance)
```

### Appendix figure — fixed effects and random-effect heterogeneity

```{r, fig.width=20, fig.height=28}
targets::tar_read(appendix_model_fixed_and_random_effects)
```

Panel A reports all general fixed-effect coefficients describing the modeled
relationship across species × experiment combinations in the seven registered
REML models, with experiment-clustered CR1 95% confidence intervals. Filled
points have intervals that exclude zero. Panel B reports the five
species-level random components as standard deviations, obtained by taking the
square root of each variance estimate and its profile-likelihood confidence
limits. A profile interval is found by fixing one variance component at a
sequence of candidate values, re-optimizing the remaining model parameters,
and retaining values whose loss in log likelihood is within the 95%
likelihood-ratio cutoff. These constrained optimizations quantify uncertainty
around the existing primary fit; they do not replace that model.
Random-component interval support indicates between-species heterogeneity, not
a nonzero general fixed-effect slope.

### Performance interpretation boundary

General fixed-effect performance for held-out species × experiment
combinations is the primary generalization result. Repeat-species performance
answers the narrower question of whether responses improve when a species has
already been observed in other gradients. Held-out effects outside the training
climate hull remain in the global score and are also available as an explicitly
flagged sensitivity stratum.

### Additional principal objects

`model_fit_r2`, `model_cross_validation_predictions`, `model_cross_validation_metrics`, `model_predictive_skill`, `model_performance_validation`, `model_fixed_effects`, `model_random_effect_profiles`, `model_random_effect_correlations`, and `model_effects_validation`.

The predictive-performance release gate additionally requires all 200 fold fits to converge without rank reduction, every predictive covariance to be positive definite, exact train/test covariance separation, finite metric and bootstrap estimates, and valid interval coverage.
